body.objective: Students will be able to use proportion to draw the figure.
body.iCan: I can use proportion to draw the figure.
successCriteria: I can use the head as a unit to measure body proportions
I can locate key landmarks on the figure
I can draw a proportioned figure from observation
body.hook: Most beginners draw heads too big and legs too short. Artists since ancient Greece have used a simple trick: measure the body in "heads." An adult is about seven and a half heads tall, and once you know the landmarks, figures start to look right.

vocabulary.definition: The size of parts compared to each other and to the whole.
The height of the head, used to measure the body.
A key point on the body used to check proportion, such as the elbow or knee.
Measuring a model by holding a pencil at arm's length.

study.title: Measuring the Figure
study.question: How do artists draw the human body in proportion?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Proportion guide (adult figure, about 7½ to 8 heads tall): head = 1; chin to nipples ≈ 1 more; navel ≈ 3 heads down; hip joint and crotch ≈ 4 (the middle of the body); knees ≈ 6; feet at 7½ to 8. Elbows line up with the waist; wrists line up with the crotch; the shoulders are about 2 heads wide. Teenagers are often about 7 heads tall.
2. Proportion chart (15 minutes): Draw a vertical line and divide it into 8 equal head units. Draw a simple figure of ovals and lines that fits the landmarks.
3. Sighting (25 minutes): A classmate poses standing (fully clothed, simple pose) for 10 minutes at a time. Hold your pencil at arm's length, measure the head with your thumb, then count how many heads tall the model is. Draw the figure lightly, checking landmarks.
Note: in Grade 9 we draw clothed classmates, mannequins and figures from photos.

body.objective: Students will be able to capture movement with gesture drawing.
body.iCan: I can capture movement with gesture drawing.
successCriteria: I can draw quick gestures that capture movement
I can use a line of action to show energy
I can build a figure from gesture to form
body.hook: Watch a dancer or a soccer player and try to draw them. They move too fast for details. Gesture drawing captures the action in 30 seconds: not the eyelashes, but the swing, twist and energy of the whole body.

vocabulary.definition: A fast drawing that captures the movement and pose of a figure.
An imaginary curved line running through the figure that shows its main movement.
A pose where weight rests on one leg, tilting the hips and shoulders in opposite directions.
Moving the body's weight from one leg to another.
A pose held for a set time, such as 30 seconds or 2 minutes.
A simple figure of lines used as a first step.

study.title: Capture the Motion
study.question: How can quick drawings capture movement?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Look: Study Edgar Degas's ballet dancers (1870s–1880s) and the ancient Greek sculpture Doryphoros, an early example of contrapposto.
2. Line of action (5 minutes): For each of five photos of athletes, draw only the one curved line that shows the main movement.
3. 30-second gestures (10 minutes): Classmates take turns holding action poses (throwing, reaching, kicking, dancing) for 30 seconds. Draw the line of action first, then the head, ribcage and hips as simple shapes, then quick limbs. Don't erase.
4. Longer poses (15 minutes): Three 2-minute poses. Add proportion checks to the gesture.
5. Contrapposto (10 minutes): One 5-minute standing pose with weight on one leg. Notice how the hips tilt one way and shoulders the other.

body.objective: Students will be able to draw a portrait using facial proportions.
body.iCan: I can draw a portrait using facial proportions.
successCriteria: I can use facial proportions to place features
I can draw a portrait from observation
I can use value to model the face
body.hook: Most people draw eyes near the top of the head. In reality, the eyes sit halfway down. Once you know a few facial proportions, your portraits start to look like real people instead of cartoons.

vocabulary.definition: An artwork showing a person, especially the face.
The guidelines for where features sit on the face.
The eyes, nose, mouth and ears.
A portrait an artist makes of themselves.
A view of the face turned partly to the side.
How much a portrait looks like the real person.

study.title: Face to Face
study.question: How do facial proportions help me draw a convincing portrait?
study.passage:
Facial proportion guide (front view, written for this lesson):
Draw an egg shape. A horizontal line halfway down is the eye line.
The face is about five eyes wide, with one eye's width between the eyes.
The bottom of the nose is about halfway between the eye line and the chin.
The mouth is about one-third of the way from the nose to the chin. The corners of the mouth line up with the centres of the eyes.
The ears sit between the eye line (or eyebrows) and the bottom of the nose.
The hairline is about halfway between the eye line and the top of the head; hair adds volume above the skull.
Studio steps: 1. Draw a proportion guide face (15 minutes). 2. Self-portrait from a mirror (35 minutes): lightly draw the guidelines, place features, then use value to show the shadows under the brow, nose and chin. 3. Compare: does it look like you? Which feature gives the strongest likeness?
